name: Kupup
tagline: Elephant Lake and an army golf course below the old Jelep La
meta_description: Kupup on the Silk Route: Bitang Tso or Elephant Lake, the Yak Golf Course, the old Jelep La trade road, permits, road links to Zuluk and Tsomgo.
summary: Kupup is an army hamlet at about 3,950–4,000 m in East Sikkim, below the Dongkya Range close to Jelep La. Travellers stop for Bitang Tso, the Elephant Lake, and the army's Yak Golf Course, on the Silk Route between Gnathang and Tsomgo. It needs a Silk Route permit and a car; there is nowhere to sleep.

local_story.title: Below Jelep La, the lovely level pass
paras: Kupup lies in a valley below the Dongkya Range, a few kilometres from Jelep La, the pass that carried more trade between India and Tibet than any other in the Raj era. Mule trains came up from Kalimpong through Pedong, Rongli, Zuluk and Gnathang, rested near here, then crossed Jelep La into the Chumbi valley and on towards Lhasa. Wool came south for Kalimpong's warehouses; cloth, tools, sugar and tea went north.

In 1888 British troops pushed Tibetan forces back over these passes, and in 1903–04 Younghusband's column came this way towards Lhasa. After 1959 the trade thinned, and after the 1962 war Jelep La was closed for good. Kupup became an army post on a sensitive frontier. A border road from Kupup now leads to Doka La, near the disputed Doklam plateau, where Indian and Chinese troops faced each other for over two months in 2017.

Kupup's most famous sight is a lake. A moraine ridge across the valley forms part of the watershed between the Teesta and the Dichu rivers, and below it lies Bitang Tso, which the army and travellers call the Elephant Lake for its shape when seen from the road above. It is conventionally held to be the source of the Dichu. Beside it, on rare flat ground, the army laid out a golf course.

did_you_know: Bitang Tso, the Elephant Lake at Kupup, is conventionally held to be the source of the Dichu river; a moraine ridge nearby divides the Teesta and Dichu basins.
Jelep La, a few kilometres from Kupup, is only about 4.8 km from Nathu La; it was the main Kalimpong–Lhasa trade pass until the border closed after 1962.
A border road from Kupup leads to Doka La, near the Doklam plateau, scene of a standoff between Indian and Chinese troops from June to August 2017.
intro: Kupup is not a village in the usual sense: a scatter of army buildings, a few huts and the road, in an open, windswept valley at about 4,000 m. Travellers see it on the Silk Route, usually on the day they drive from Zuluk or Gnathang towards Tsomgo and Gangtok, or as an out-and-back from Gnathang. The reason to stop is the view of Bitang Tso, the Elephant Lake, below the road, and the army's Yak Golf Course on the flat ground nearby.

This is high, cold and restricted country. Indian travellers need the Silk Route permit, arranged at Rongli or by a Gangtok operator, and a registered Sikkim car; foreign nationals face tighter and changing rules. Snow can cover Kupup from December to April and close the road. There is no tourist accommodation, so sleep at Gnathang or Zuluk below, or return to Gangtok. Check current status before you travel.
facts: Elephant Lake, Yak Golf Course, Jelep La
None for most of the way
costs: Reserved SUV for the Silk Route
Small fee; agent may charge for arranging it
Tea or noodles at an army or roadside stall, where open
Homestay at Gnathang with dinner and breakfast
Boot and coat hire in Gangtok or on the way

highlights.title: Bitang Tso, the Elephant Lake
highlights.text: Seen from the road above, this small glacial lake has the outline of an elephant, trunk and all, which is why everyone calls it the Elephant Lake. It is conventionally held to be the source of the Dichu river. It freezes in winter and turns deep blue on clear autumn days.

highlights.title: The Yak Golf Course
highlights.text: On a flat stretch of valley floor near Kupup, the army maintains the Yak Golf Course, often described as one of the highest golf courses in the world. You see it from the road; playing is for army guests. It makes an odd and memorable sight in this bare country.

highlights.title: The old Jelep La road
highlights.text: Kupup lies a few kilometres below Jelep La, the main pass of the Kalimpong–Lhasa wool trade until 1962. Tourists cannot go to the pass, but the valley gives a sense of the route the mule trains climbed. Ask your driver to point out its direction.

highlights.title: The crossing to Tsomgo
highlights.text: From Kupup the road climbs over a shoulder to join the Nathu La road near the new Baba Mandir, then descends past Tsomgo Lake to Gangtok. It turns the Silk Route into a loop and avoids doubling back through Zuluk and Rongli. Permits and road status decide whether you can.

highlights.title: High-altitude country
highlights.text: Around Kupup the land is above the tree line: rock, scree, alpine grass and small lakes, with yaks grazing in summer. On clear days the snow ridges of the Dongkya Range stand behind. The light is harsh and the wind strong; this is no place for long walks.

how_to_reach.mode: Reserved SUV on the Silk Route
how_to_reach.text: Most travellers reach Kupup in an SUV hired for the Silk Route, at ₹5,000–7,000 a day, coming up from Zuluk and Gnathang. The operator or homestay arranges the Rongli permit with photo ID copies and passport photos. Kupup is about 15–20 km beyond Gnathang.

Some operators run Kupup from Gangtok via Tsomgo and Baba Mandir, about 70 km and 3–3.5 hours, as a long day trip or the first leg of a reverse Silk Route loop. It depends on the permits that season. Check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: There is no tourist accommodation at Kupup; it is an army area, and travellers pass through. The nearest beds are the family homestays of Gnathang, about 15–20 km away, at around 3,800–4,000 m, where you get a simple room, heavy quilts and dinner and breakfast for about ₹1,200–2,000 per person. Lower and warmer, Zuluk's homestays are another hour beyond. If you come via Tsomgo, return to Gangtok for the night, where budget rooms and family guesthouses are easy to find.
tips: Sleep at least one night at Zuluk or Padamchen before reaching Kupup, rather than driving up from Gangtok or Rongli in one go.
Carry extra copies of your photo ID and passport photos; army posts on this stretch check documents.
Do not photograph army camps, vehicles or soldiers without permission.
Keep stops at Kupup short, drink water and turn back if anyone has a severe headache or feels confused.
Ask your driver before the trip whether the crossing from Kupup to Tsomgo is open on your permit.

experiences.title: Elephant Lake from the road above Kupup
experiences.cost: Included in your Silk Route car
experiences.summary: From the road near Kupup, look down on Bitang Tso, a small glacial lake shaped like an elephant, held to be the source of the Dichu river. It is a short stop on the Silk Route, best on clear days when the water turns deep blue.
body: Bitang Tso lies in a hollow below the road near Kupup, on the far side of a moraine ridge that forms part of the watershed between the Teesta and Dichu rivers. From the right point above, its outline looks like an elephant, with a long trunk curling off one end, and that is the name everyone uses. It is conventionally held to be the source of the Dichu, which flows east through the Chumbi side of the border.

Drivers know the viewpoint and stop on request. On a clear day in October or November the lake is deep blue against brown grass and grey scree; in April and May the snow around it is melting; from December to March it is usually frozen and white. The shape shows best from a little height, so stay on the road edge rather than walking down to the shore, which is an army area and very cold.

At about 4,000 m even this short stop takes effort. Walk slowly from the car, keep your hat and gloves on and do not linger in the wind. Photography of the lake is generally fine, but do not point cameras at the army installations around Kupup. If cloud is down, which happens often in the afternoon, the lake may not be visible at all.

faqs.q: Why is it called Elephant Lake?
faqs.a: Seen from the road above Kupup, Bitang Tso's outline looks like an elephant, with a long trunk at one end. Travellers and soldiers call it the Elephant Lake for that reason. The shape shows best from a little height on a clear day, and is lost in snow when the lake freezes.

faqs.q: Can we walk down to Elephant Lake?
faqs.a: Usually no. The shore lies in an army area and visitors view the lake from the road. The ground is also boggy in summer and icy in winter, and walking at 4,000 m is hard work. Stay on the road edge, take your photographs and move on.

faqs.q: When is the Elephant Lake frozen?
faqs.a: Bitang Tso usually freezes from about December to March and can keep ice into April. The road to Kupup may be closed by snow in the same months. For the blue water, come in October and November, or in May once the ice has gone. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: The army's Yak Golf Course
experiences.cost: Free to view from the road
experiences.summary: On a rare flat stretch of valley near Kupup, the Indian Army keeps the Yak Golf Course, often described as one of the highest golf courses in the world. Visitors see it from the road. It is a strange, memorable sight among rock and snow.
body: Flat ground is scarce at 4,000 m, and on one of the few level stretches near Kupup the Indian Army laid out a golf course for its officers and guests. It is known as the Yak Golf Course, and it is often described, including by the army, as one of the highest golf courses in the world. The fairways are rough alpine grass, the greens are small, and in winter the whole course disappears under snow.

Tourists usually see it only from the road, where drivers stop for photographs. Playing is not open to the public; it is managed by the army for its own people and invited guests. Do not walk onto the course or into the army area around it, and ask before photographing anything near the camp.

The stop is short but it adds a wry note to a day of passes, lakes and memorials. Combine it with the Elephant Lake viewpoint nearby, and keep the visit to a few minutes: the wind here is cold in every month, and at this height you will feel short of breath just walking back to the car.

faqs.q: Can tourists play golf at Kupup?
faqs.a: No. The Yak Golf Course is run by the Indian Army for its officers and invited guests, and is not open to the public. Tourists view it from the road. Do not walk onto the course or into the surrounding army area.

faqs.q: Is the Yak Golf Course the highest in the world?
faqs.a: It is often described as one of the highest golf courses in the world, at about 4,000 m. Claims about the highest course vary, and we would not treat any single claim as settled. Either way, it is a remarkable place to see a golf course.

faqs.q: Is the Yak Golf Course on the way to Tsomgo?
faqs.a: It is near Kupup, on the Silk Route between Gnathang and the Nathu La road. If your permit and car allow the crossing from Kupup to Tsomgo, you pass it on the way. It is not on the standard Gangtok–Tsomgo day trip, which turns back before Kupup.

experiences.title: Looking up the old road to Jelep La
experiences.duration: 30 minutes, as part of the drive
experiences.summary: Kupup lies a few kilometres below Jelep La, the pass that carried the wool trade between Lhasa and Kalimpong until 1962. Tourists cannot go up to it, but from the valley you can trace where mule trains climbed. A short stop for history rather than scenery alone.
body: For most of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Jelep La was the busiest trade pass between India and Tibet. The route ran from Kalimpong through Pedong, Rhenock and Rongli, up through Zuluk and Gnathang, past Kupup and over Jelep La into the Chumbi valley, then on to Phari and Lhasa. Mules and ponies carried bales of Tibetan wool down; cloth, metal goods, sugar and tea went up. Kalimpong's wool merchants grew rich on it.

The pass was also a military gate. British forces crossed it in 1888, after fighting Tibetan troops at Lingtu and Gnathang, and again in 1903–04 with Younghusband's expedition. After the events in Tibet in 1959 the trade thinned, and after the 1962 war the pass was closed. Today it is a military area, and tourists are not allowed beyond the road at Kupup.

Stand by the road near Kupup on a clear morning and ask your driver to point towards Jelep La on the ridge above. It is easy to picture the mule trains coming down that slope after days on the Tibetan plateau. Combine the stop with the Elephant Lake view, and keep it short. Read Zuluk's and Gnathang's stories, too: they are the same road.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit Jelep La?
faqs.a: No. Jelep La is a closed border pass in a military area, and tourists may not go beyond the road near Kupup. You can see the direction of the pass from the valley and learn its story, but no permit currently allows visitors to the top. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Jelep La from Nathu La?
faqs.a: Jelep La and Nathu La are only about 4.8 km apart in a straight line, both on the Dongkya Range between Sikkim and the Chumbi valley of Tibet. Nathu La is open to Indian tourists on set days; Jelep La is not. Both carried trade to Lhasa before 1962.

faqs.q: What was traded over Jelep La?
faqs.a: Tibetan wool was the main export south, along with yak tails, musk and salt, much of it bound for Kalimpong's warehouses. Northbound loads included cloth, metal goods, sugar and tea. The trade thinned after 1959 and stopped when the border closed after the 1962 war.

experiences.title: Over the top from Kupup to Tsomgo
experiences.cost: Part of a ₹5,000–7,000 a day SUV
experiences.summary: From Kupup the Silk Route climbs over a shoulder to meet the Nathu La road near the new Baba Mandir, then drops past Tsomgo Lake to Gangtok. It closes the Silk Route loop and saves the long drive back through Zuluk and Rongli, if permits and snow allow.
body: Most Silk Route trips go up through Rongli and Zuluk and come back the same way. If your permit and your car's papers allow, there is a better finish: carry on from Kupup over the high ground to the junction with the Nathu La road near the new Baba Mandir, stop at the shrine, then descend past Tsomgo Lake and through the Kyongnosla forest to Gangtok. It saves several hours of doubling back and adds two more sights to the day.

The road over the top is high and exposed, with long stretches above 4,000 m, and snow can block it from December to April. Your driver will know whether it is open; ask the evening before at your Gnathang or Zuluk homestay. Some permits cover only the Rongli route, so confirm with the operator when you book. In some seasons the loop is run in reverse, starting from Gangtok via Tsomgo.

Leave early, eat breakfast before you go and carry water and snacks, since there is little on the way. Stop at Baba Mandir for half an hour and at Tsomgo for tea and a short walk. You should reach Gangtok in the early afternoon. If anyone feels unwell at height, the descent past Tsomgo is the quickest way down. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can we return from the Silk Route to Gangtok via Tsomgo?
faqs.a: Often yes. From Kupup the road joins the Nathu La road near Baba Mandir and descends past Tsomgo to Gangtok. Whether you may take it depends on your permit, your car's papers and snow. Ask your operator when you book and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long is the drive from Kupup to Gangtok?
faqs.a: About 70 km and 3–3.5 hours via Baba Mandir and Tsomgo, plus stops. If you start from Gnathang, add about an hour. The route back through Zuluk and Rongli is longer, about 120 km and 5–6 hours, so the Tsomgo crossing saves much of a day.

faqs.q: Is the Kupup crossing open in winter?
faqs.a: Often not. Snow can close the high road between Kupup and the Nathu La road from December to April, sometimes for weeks. Drivers then return via Zuluk and Rongli. Keep a spare day, ask your homestay the evening before, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit to visit Kupup?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian travellers need the Silk Route permit, which covers Zuluk, Gnathang and Kupup, arranged at Rongli or through a registered Gangtok operator with photo ID copies and passport photos. Foreign nationals face separate, tighter rules that change often. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How high is Kupup?
faqs.a: Kupup lies at about 3,950–4,000 m, more than 2,300 m above Gangtok and about 1,000 m above Zuluk. Breathlessness and headaches are common. Sleep a night lower down first, walk slowly and keep stops short. Go down at once if anyone feels faint, confused or very sick.

faqs.q: How do we get to Kupup from Gangtok?
faqs.a: Either via Tsomgo and Baba Mandir, about 70 km and 3–3.5 hours, if the permit allows, or via Rongli, Zuluk and Gnathang, about 120 km, usually over two days with a night at Zuluk. Most people hire an SUV for the Silk Route at ₹5,000–7,000 a day.

faqs.q: Can we stay overnight at Kupup?
faqs.a: No, there is no tourist accommodation at Kupup, which is an army area. Stay at the homestays of Gnathang, about 15–20 km away, for ₹1,200–2,000 per person with meals, or lower down at Zuluk. Coming via Tsomgo, return to Gangtok for the night.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Kupup?
faqs.a: October and November give clear skies and blue water at the Elephant Lake; April and May bring melting snow and longer days. December to March is very cold, with the lake frozen and the road often closed by snow. The monsoon months bring cloud and landslides.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Kupup?
faqs.a: Rules for foreign nationals on the Silk Route, including Kupup, are stricter than for Indians and have changed several times. Foreigners need a Restricted Area Permit for Sikkim and may need a further permit through a registered agent, if access is allowed at all. Ask a Gangtok agent and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Kupup on the Nathu La day trip?
faqs.a: Not usually. The standard Gangtok day trip goes to Tsomgo, Nathu La and the new Baba Mandir, and turns back before Kupup. Kupup is reached on the Silk Route or on a special permit via Tsomgo. Ask your operator if you want to include it.

faqs.q: Is there food at Kupup?
faqs.a: Very little. An army-run or roadside stall may sell tea, coffee and instant noodles in season, but do not rely on it. Carry water, biscuits, dry fruit and a flask of tea from your homestay. Eat breakfast before you set out for the day.

faqs.q: Is Kupup safe for children and older travellers?
faqs.a: Healthy children and fit older travellers who have slept a night at Zuluk usually manage a short stop. Infants and anyone with heart or lung problems should not go up without medical advice. Keep everyone warm and hydrated, stay briefly and turn back if anyone feels unwell.
